correctness.rationale: For every finite projective plane of order \(q\ge2\), the exact q+1 incidence and unique-join axioms give four positive two-vertex incidence counts \(1,q,q,q(q-1)\). Duplicator preserves sides, incidence and an optional common-neighbour predicate for distinct homogeneous triples after three rounds. The full case split for the fourth choice gives the same equality/adjacency diagrams in every plane: for collinear triples 111 and singletons; for noncollinear triples doubletons and singletons; for mixed triples all permitted fresh patterns, with 11 only when the selected opposite-side vertex is not the unique join. A same-side fresh vertex supplies 000 in both cases, including the order-two edge case. This is a complete arbitrary-plane Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse proof, not a finite extrapolation. The rank-five formula for a degree-at-least-four vertex has five quantifiers and separates the degree-three Heawood graph from every order-\(q\ge3\) plane. The C++ exact rank-four type recursion for prime orders 2,3,5 and independently implemented Python local-triple extension checks for orders 2,3 were rerun from the supplied source files and agree.

originality.rationale: The mathematically closest accessible preceding projective-plane statement concerns point/line-named incidence, where the binary and ternary orders separate at rank four. That separation does not imply pure adjacency equivalence; a side-labelled quantifier over points cannot be simulated with the same rank in the uncoloured graph. Published general graph EF upper bounds and two-sorted modal axiomatizations likewise do not imply this uniform pure-graph four-round collapse. Search of published mathematical findings and accessible prior scientific claims found no covering statement. An accessible full text of the same-object modal article was not obtained, so historical priority is not certified.

value.rationale: This is a natural complete quantifier-rank-four classification of all finite projective-plane Levi incidence graphs, including non-Desarguesian planes and unbounded orders, represented sharply by the 14-vertex Heawood graph. A nontrivial fourth-move extension lemma explains how loss of unary side predicates hides the binary-vs-ternary projective-plane difference that is detectable at rank four in named-sort incidence logic. At rank five the degree >=4 sentence detects the Fano plane exactly, giving a sharp logical-visibility boundary rather than a routine finite table or small numerical improvement.
